intro: My research is in graph theory and combinatorics, with an emphasis on spectral and extremal questions. I also work on Fourier analysis and its connections to graph theory and additive combinatorics.

projects.title: Brualdi–Solheid problem
paragraphs: The Brualdi–Solheid problem asks which graphs have the largest or smallest spectral radius within a given class. My work has focused on minimization, with either the order and size or the order and dissociation number fixed.

The fixed-order-and-size problem is related to a question of Hong on whether a minimizer must be almost regular. The dissociation-number problem connects spectral minimization with Turán-type problems for complete multipartite graphs.

projects.title: Associahedron
paragraphs: The associahedron graph has a vertex for each triangulation of a convex polygon. Two triangulations are adjacent when a single diagonal flip changes one into the other.

With Sebastian Cioabă, I obtained a lower bound for its smallest adjacency eigenvalue with the correct order of magnitude. The proof uses a more general eigenvalue bound for regular graphs containing many copies of a fixed subgraph.

projects.title: Spectral Moore bounds
paragraphs: How many vertices can a connected regular graph have if its degree is fixed and its second largest adjacency eigenvalue is bounded above? This is the spectral Moore problem.
With Sebastian Cioabă, Hiroshi Nozaki, and Ziqing Xiang, I studied bounds and equality cases for small degrees and eigenvalue thresholds, as well as the non-existence of certain Moore polygons.
projects.highlight: One result is a gap in the possible second largest eigenvalues of connected 5-regular graphs: if λ₂ > 1, then λ₂ ≥ √5 − 1. Up to isomorphism, the Cayley graph shown here is the only graph attaining equality.

projects.title: Fourier analysis of graphs
paragraphs: After labeling the vertices of a graph by ℤ_N, its adjacency matrix can be viewed as a function on ℤ_N². The Fourier transform depends on the labeling, even though the underlying graph does not change.

Our work studies the Fourier ratio—the ratio of the ℓ¹ and ℓ² norms of this transform—and its minimum over all vertex labelings, which we call the edge complexity of the graph. The questions include its relation to graph energy and additive structure, the labelings that attain equality in energy bounds, and approximation from incomplete observations.

figures.alt: Alternating labeling of K four four, with its Fourier transform and Fourier ratio 1.414
Consecutive labeling of K four four, with its Fourier transform and Fourier ratio 3.121

projects.caption: Two labelings of K₄,₄ give Fourier ratios approximately 1.414 and 3.121. The images show the magnitudes of the Fourier transforms, on the same color scale. These are direct calculations for the displayed labelings, not a claim that both labelings are optimal.

projects.title: Ricci curvature
paragraphs: Effective resistance comes from viewing a graph as an electrical network. It also gives a way to define curvature on a graph.

With collaborators, I introduced Ricci–Foster curvature on edges and studied the resulting Ricci flow. We proved short-time existence and preservation of nonnegative and positive curvature. In a separate paper, we studied node resistance curvature under Cartesian graph products, including its signs at interior and boundary vertices of grid graphs.
